transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland
says he will challenge Senator Chuck Schumer
for the role of Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress.
That's when Democrats are back in the majority in the House and Senate.
NPR's Luke Garrett reports.
In a statement, Senator Van Hollen said Americans called for change
at the ballot box, and that means new leadership in the Senate.
Senator-elect Abdul Said told NPR he supports Van Hollen,
citing his "righteous fights" against the Trump administration.
Schumer does maintain support within his caucus.
Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who votes with Democrats,
endorsed Schumer and called him the architect
of the most successful election in modern history.
Democratic Senate leadership elections are set for early December.
Luke Garrett, NPR News, Washington.
As Democrats prepare to retake control of Congress in January,
voter turnout in the midterms was historically high,
as NPR's Domenico Montanaro reports.
Turnout in this election was almost a record.
According to the University of Florida election lab,
which tracks turnout, 49.1 percent of eligible voters
cast ballots across the country in this year's midterm elections.
That's just a tick lower than the 50 percent who showed up to vote in 2018,
which was the highest mark in more than 100 years.
The states that saw the highest turnout were Maine, Michigan, and Minnesota.
The lowest were Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Tennessee.
The overall turnout in this election represented a trend during the Trump era
of higher-than-usual midterm participation,
but it was still 24 percent lower than the 2024 presidential election.
Domenico Montanaro, NPR News, Washington.
NVIDIA's chief financial officer is now acting as the AI computer chip company's interim CEO.
This follows the resignation of Jensen Huang less than a week after the CEO
and co-founder acknowledged an affair with a reported Chinese spy.
NPR has not confirmed those reports.
NPR's Shannon Bond has more.
Colette Crass has worked at NVIDIA since 2013.
She helped oversee its transformation from a video game chipmaker
to arguably the central player in the artificial intelligence industry
and one of the world's most valuable companies.
In a statement, she said she is "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created."
Jensen Huang's sudden departure has put a spotlight on the company's lack of succession planning.
NVIDIA's board says it's launching a search for a permanent CEO
and will consider internal and external candidates.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
In New York, authorities say the search has ended for more victims of Wednesday's building collapse in Brooklyn.
Eight people were killed when a three-story structure containing apartments and commercial space gave way
as construction workers were excavating the lot next door.
The cause of the collapse remains under investigation.
Wall Street futures are mostly higher this morning.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Police in Washington, D.C. say the man who fatally shot one person
and wounded four others yesterday in a neighborhood north of the White House was a doctor.
He's identified as 55-year-old Matt Lambert.
Police say Lambert took his own life after the shootings.
The interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department says Lambert had been in a long-running legal dispute
over conditions in his penthouse condo.
The person killed was shot at a local gym and was identified as the manager of Lambert's condo building.
Microsoft says it's still working to fix a major outage that's affecting individual users, companies, and government operations.
NPR's Catherine Welch says the outage began yesterday in the early afternoon Eastern time.
The outage tracker down detector shows reports suddenly spiked at nearly 130,000 users at around 1 p.m. Eastern,
with thousands more coming in as the day went on.
The outage kept users from accessing email through Outlook or sending message over Teams
and affected other apps in the Microsoft Office suite.
It's not clear what prompted the outage, but in updates on social media,
Microsoft said it was aware that users were encountering issues in "multiple connection methods" in the Americas.
We should note Microsoft is a financial supporter of NPR.
The company has been providing updates on social media and said it was trying several fixes.
Catherine Welch, NPR News.
Plus at plus.npr.org. That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland says he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
U.S. midterm voter turnout reaches 49.1 percent, nearly matching the record set in 2018
NVIDIA CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigns over reported affair with Chinese spy
Search continues to confirm additional victims of Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight
Washington, D.C. shooting leaves one dead and four wounded; suspect Dr. Matt Lambert dies by suicide
Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams, and Office apps across the Americas for users and governments
